full_text_en:
Su Xiangqian v. Xuzhou Baixin Commercial Co., Ltd., Baihui Supermarket Branch, and Xuzhou Baixin Commercial Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of consumer rights and interests

Ruling Summary

Product labeling constitutes the fundamental basis for consumers to understand and judge the characteristics, value, suitability, and utility of a product, and is an important source of information for consumers to choose and decide whether to purchase a product. Pursuant to Article 5 of the Product Quality Law of the People's Republic of China, a seller shall ensure the truthfulness of the contents of product labels, which represent the minimum standard of the seller's duty of truthfulness owed to consumers. If a consumer suffers damage due to untrue contents recorded on product labels, the business operator shall bear corresponding liability in accordance with the law.

Plaintiff: Su Xiangqian, male, 69 years old, Han ethnicity, retired worker of Xuzhou No. 25 Middle School, residing at the teacher's dormitory building of Xuzhou No. 24 Middle School, Gulou District, Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Xuzhou Baixin Commercial Co., Ltd., Baihui Supermarket Branch, domiciled at East Qingnian Road, Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province.
Person in charge: Zhou Fumin, Manager of the Branch.

Defendant: Xuzhou Baixin Commercial Co., Ltd., domiciled at East Qingnian Road, Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province.
Legal representative: Zhou Fumin, General Manager of the Company.

Plaintiff Su Xiangqian commenced this action against Defendant Xuzhou Baixin Commercial Co., Ltd., Baihui Supermarket Branch (hereinafter referred to as Baihui Branch) and Xuzhou Baixin Commercial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Baixin Company) for a dispute over infringement of consumer rights and interests, and filed the lawsuit with the Yunlong District People's Court of Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province.

Plaintiff's Allegations:
On April 12, 2010, the Plaintiff purchased 8 boxes of Tieguanyin tea from Defendant Baihui Branch, spending a total of RMB 3,840. In 2011, the Xiaoshan Branch of the Hangzhou Municipal Bureau of Quality and Technical Supervision identified the tea in question as counterfeit. On March 15 of the same year, upon investigation by the Xiaoshan District Health Bureau of Hangzhou, the hygiene license of the manufacturer of the tea in question was found to be forged. The Plaintiff requested the court to order the Defendants to compensate for the file retrieval fee of RMB 100, the loss of tea of RMB 3,840, and to pay ten times the compensation amount of RMB 38,400, and that the litigation costs be borne by the Defendants.

Defendants' Defense:
The Defendants argued that the tea sold was not counterfeit, had a production license, and met safety standards. The mislabeling was due to a staff error where the manufacturer label of Fujian Anxi County Chaotianyan Tea Factory was mistakenly replaced with the label of Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd. The hygiene license number affixed to the Tieguanyin tea was that of the Longjing tea produced by Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd. which the Defendant sold. The Defendant sold Tieguanyin, and the consumer also intended to purchase Tieguanyin; in this regard, the Defendant was not at fault, and the consumer suffered no actual or potential interest damage. The Plaintiff failed to prove that the tea sold by the Defendant violated the food safety provisions of Article 96 of the Food Safety Law of the People's Republic of China. Therefore, the Defendants requested the dismissal of the Plaintiff's claims.

The Yunlong District People's Court of Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province found the following facts at first instance:

On April 12, 2010, Plaintiff Su Xiangqian purchased 8 boxes of "Guanyin King" (a grade of Tieguanyin tea) from Defendant Baihui Branch, spending a total of RMB 3,840. The tea bags were only marked with "Tieguanyin" and similar identifiers, while the outer packaging box bore the words "Guanyin King" and "China · Anxi" on the front, and on the back, a product label was affixed with adhesive, stating: Seller, Baihui Supermarket; Brand, Jujia; Hygiene License, Xiaoshan Food Production Word (2003) No. 0094; Manufacturer, Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd.; and a quality safety mark. The price tag stated: Tieguanyin tea, price RMB 480 per box. On March 14, 2011, the Xiaoshan Branch of the Hangzhou Municipal Bureau of Quality and Technical Supervision issued a "Reply on the Report of Food Production License Issues of Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd.", stating: "The Tieguanyin tea purchased on April 12, 2010 at the Baihui Supermarket of Xuzhou Baixin Commercial Co., Ltd., labeled as manufacturer Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd., with a production date of April 10, 2010, was identified by the company as not being produced by it. The reason is that the company's identification information is printed directly on the outer packaging of the product, not affixed by adhesive." On March 15 of the same year, the Xiaoshan District Health Bureau of Hangzhou issued a "Reply on the Inquiry Letter Regarding the 'Hygiene License Number'", stating: "The number 'Xiaoshan Food Production Word (2003) No. 0094' clearly does not conform to the numbering rules for issuing licenses. Furthermore, upon searching the license archives, no hygiene license with the above number was found to have been issued. The hygiene license issued to Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd. bore the number 'Xiaoshan Health Food Production Word (2003) No. 0094'." Defendant Baihui Branch also sold Tieguanyin tea produced by Fujian Anxi County Chaotianyan Tea Factory and marketed by Guangzhou Chaotianyan Tea Co., Ltd.

Separately, as of the conclusion of the trial, only 4 boxes of the 8 boxes of Tieguanyin tea purchased by Plaintiff Su Xiangqian remained due to reasons such as inspection. Although the Plaintiff alleged that the tea did not meet food safety standards and was toxic, he failed to provide evidence to prove this.

The issues in dispute at first instance were: 1. Whether the Defendants Baihui Branch and Baixin Company's act of mislabeling the product label constituted fraud; 2. Whether the tea sold by the Defendants met food safety standards, and whether the tenfold penalty rule applied.

The Yunlong District People's Court of Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province held at first instance:

1. The act of mislabeling the product label by Defendants Baihui Branch and Baixin Company constituted fraud. The "Reply on the Report of Food Production License Issues of Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd." issued by the Xiaoshan Branch of the Hangzhou Municipal Bureau of Quality and Technical Supervision confirmed that the product label affixed to the Tieguanyin tea sold by the Defendants recorded a manufacturer inconsistent with the actual manufacturer; the identified manufacturer, Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd., was verified not to have produced this type of tea. The "Reply on the Inquiry Letter Regarding the 'Hygiene License Number'" issued by the Xiaoshan District Health Bureau of Hangzhou proved that the hygiene license number of Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd. stated on the label, "Xiaoshan Food Production Word (2003) No. 0094", was also nonexistent.

Pursuant to Articles 5, 37, and 38 of the Product Quality Law of the People's Republic of China, sellers are prohibited from forging or fraudulently using quality marks such as certification marks; they are prohibited from forging the place of origin of products, or forging or fraudulently using the names and addresses of other manufacturers. Defendants Baihui Branch and Baixin Company, as professional supermarket operators, should have recognized that the contents of product labels on the goods they sell must be truthful. When selling the Tieguanyin tea in question, they failed to verify the product label affixed to the outer packaging, resulting in the fraudulent use of another party's product label. Plaintiff Su Xiangqian relied on the trust in the product label provided by the Defendants when purchasing the tea. Therefore, the Defendants, as business operators, made misrepresentations regarding their business conduct, and thus their act of mislabeling the product label constituted fraud.

2. There was no evidence that the tea in question sold by Defendants Baihui Branch and Baixin Company did not meet food safety standards, thus the tenfold penalty rule did not apply. Pursuant to the second paragraph of Article 96 of the Food Safety Law of the People's Republic of China, if a producer produces food that does not meet food safety standards, or a seller knowingly sells food that does not meet food safety standards, the consumer may, in addition to claiming compensation for losses, demand from the producer or seller a payment of ten times the price of the food. Accordingly, for a consumer to claim tenfold compensation, they must prove that the purchased food did not meet food safety standards. Since Plaintiff Su Xiangqian failed to provide evidence that the tea in question did not meet food safety standards, or was toxic or harmful, causing acute, subacute, or chronic harm to the human body, the court did not support the Plaintiff's claim for ten times the loss.

Pursuant to Article 49 of the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests of the People's Republic of China, if a business operator engages in fraudulent conduct in providing goods or services, it shall, at the consumer's request, increase the compensation for the consumer's losses; the amount of the increased compensation shall be twice the price of the goods purchased or the cost of the services received by the consumer. Defendants Baihui Branch and Baixin Company engaged in fraudulent conduct in the sale of the tea in question. Therefore, the court supported Plaintiff Su Xiangqian's claim for compensation of the tea loss of RMB 3,840 and one-fold additional compensation of RMB 3,840. The RMB 100 spent by the Plaintiff to retrieve the business registration materials of the two Defendants was a necessary expense for this lawsuit, and the court supported the claim for compensation of this loss. Defendant Baihui Branch is a branch of Defendant Baixin Company. Pursuant to the relevant provisions of the Company Law, Defendant Baixin Company shall bear supplementary compensation liability for the above debts of Defendant Baihui Branch to the extent that Branch is unable to satisfy them. After the Plaintiff's claim for compensation for the loss of the Tieguanyin tea purchased was satisfied by Defendant Baihui Branch, the Plaintiff should return the eight boxes of tea. However, due to the Plaintiff's use for inspection and other reasons, only four boxes remained as of the conclusion of the trial. These four boxes should be returned to Defendant Baihui Branch, and the Plaintiff should compensate Defendant Baihui Branch RMB 300 for the lost value of the four boxes of Tieguanyin tea that were destroyed.

In summary, based on Articles 5, 37, and 38 of the Product Quality Law of the People's Republic of China, the second paragraph of Article 54 and Article 58 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 8 and 49 of the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests of the People's Republic of China, the first paragraph of Article 14 of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 68 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (For Trial Implementation), the Yunlong District People's Court of Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province rendered the following judgment on March 6, 2013:

1. Defendant Baihui Branch shall compensate Plaintiff Su Xiangqian for the tea loss of RMB 3,840, compensation of RMB 3,840, and file retrieval fee of RMB 100. After deducting the RMB 300 that the Plaintiff shall compensate Defendant Baihui Branch for the lost four boxes of Tieguanyin tea, the total amount to be compensated by Defendant Baihui Branch to Plaintiff Su Xiangqian is RMB 7,480, payable within seven days from the effective date of this judgment.
2. Defendant Baixin Company shall bear supplementary compensation liability to Plaintiff Su Xiangqian for the compensation amount specified in item 1 of this judgment to the extent that Defendant Baihui Branch is unable to satisfy it.
3. Plaintiff Su Xiangqian shall return the four boxes of Tieguanyin tea involved in this case to Defendant Baihui Branch within seven days from the effective date of this judgment.

Baihui Branch and Baixin Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Xuzhou Intermediate People's Court, arguing:
1. The first-instance judgment erroneously found that the Appellants constituted fraud in sales. For a seller to commit fraud against a consumer, there must be intentional misleading regarding the quality, brand, price, quantity, etc. of the product, causing the consumer to make a significantly wrong consumption choice. In this case, the Appellee, Su Xiangqian, purchased a relatively large quantity of Tieguanyin tea at one time, indicating that the Appellee was very familiar with the quality and taste of Tieguanyin tea, and thus had clear discernment regarding the authenticity, origin, grade, and labeling of the tea. Whether in packaging or in the tea itself, the Appellants clearly indicated it as Tieguanyin tea, with the origin stated as "Anxi, China". The buyer had sufficient knowledge of this information.
2. The labeling content did not constitute fraud, and the Appellants had no need to commit fraud. The Appellants admitted to mislabeling. When the Consumers' Association intervened and mediated, the Appellants had already declared the labeling error and were ordered to rectify. The Tieguanyin tea, originating from Anxi, China, was produced by the local Chaotianyan Tea Factory with complete permits, hygiene certificates, and logos. There was no necessity to counterfeit the Hangzhou Jujia Tea Factory, let alone fraudulently use Longjing logos. Such action could not achieve any misleading effect or enhance brand quality or price.
3. The statute of limitations in this case had expired. The Appellee purchased the tea on April 12, 2010, and complained to the Consumers' Association on April 13 and 14, 2010, where mediation was conducted. The Appellants clearly informed the Appellee that the label was incorrectly affixed, but there was no act of counterfeiting or intentional fraudulent use of another's label. Therefore, when the Appellee filed the lawsuit, the two-year statute of limitations had already expired. The Appellants requested the appellate court to amend the judgment according to law.

The Appellee, Su Xiangqian, responded:
1. The tea sold by the Appellants, Baihui Branch and Baixin Company, was counterfeit and substandard. The manufacturer and place of production stated on the tea were false, and the production license and safety marks were all fake.
2. The first-instance judgment correctly applied the law. The Appellants' conduct constituted fraud, and the tea was not produced by Fujian Anxi County Chaotianyan Tea Factory.
3. Regarding the statute of limitations, after purchasing the tea, the Appellee repeatedly sought negotiation with the Appellants, but the Appellants refused to address the issue. Only after the Appellee received the reply from the Xiaoshan Branch of the Hangzhou Municipal Bureau of Quality and Technical Supervision did he realize that his rights had indeed been infringed. Therefore, this case had not exceeded the statute of limitations. In summary, the Appellants' appeal lacked factual and legal basis. The Appellee requested the appellate court to dismiss the appeal and uphold the original judgment.

After the second-instance trial, the Xuzhou Intermediate People's Court confirmed the facts found at first instance.

The issues in dispute on appeal were: 1. Whether the Appellants Baihui Branch and Baixin Company's act of mislabeling the product label constituted fraud. 2. Whether the Appellee Su Xiangqian's lawsuit exceeded the statute of limitations.

The Xuzhou Intermediate People's Court held on appeal:

1. Whether the Appellants' act of mislabeling the product label constituted fraud.
    (1) Product labeling is the basic means for consumers lacking specialized knowledge to understand and judge the characteristics, value, suitability, and utility of a product, and is an important source of information for consumers to choose products and make consumption decisions. Under normal circumstances, consumers cannot solely rely on the appearance of a product to understand it. To enable consumers to fully understand and learn about a product, use it correctly, and thereby benefit from it, product labeling needs to be printed on the outer packaging. Product labeling is indispensable to consumers. Pursuant to Articles 5, 37, and 38 of the Product Quality Law of the People's Republic of China, sellers shall ensure the truthfulness of the contents of product labels, which represent the minimum standard of the seller's duty of truthfulness owed to consumers. In this case, the Appellants argued that the Appellee Su Xiangqian's one-time purchase of a relatively large quantity of Tieguanyin tea indicated that he was very familiar with the quality and taste of Tieguanyin. This inference of specialized tea knowledge based on purchase quantity is logically unfounded, and the court does not support this argument. The Appellants argued that both the packaging and the tea itself clearly indicated it as Tieguanyin tea, with the origin as "Anxi, China," and that this information alone was sufficient for the consumer's needs. However, for an ordinary consumer, the contents of the product label affixed to the tea in question not only misled the consumer in judging and understanding the tea's characteristics, value, taste, color, aroma, and other aspects of suitability and utility, but also could substantially influence the consumer's final decision to purchase. Therefore, this argument of the Appellants cannot stand.
    (2) The Appellants made false representations on the product label. The product label on the tea in question recorded the manufacturer as Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd., which was inconsistent with the actual manufacturer, Fujian Anxi County Chaotianyan Tea Factory. Moreover, the Appellants affixed a nonexistent production license number, "Xiaoshan Food Production Word (2003) No. 0094," onto the product label. Therefore, the Appellants made false representations on the product label.
    (3) The Appellants disregarded the truthfulness of their product labels. After the Appellee purchased the tea, he repeatedly sought to negotiate with the Appellants regarding the issue. However, the Appellants continued to sell Tieguanyin tea labeled as being produced by Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd. until the Appellee filed the lawsuit. Although they admitted the mislabeling during trial, the Appellants failed to take timely remedial measures despite knowing the untruthful contents of the product labels. Therefore, the Appellants disregarded the truthfulness of their product labels.
    (4) The Appellee relied on the Appellants' product label and purchased the tea. Product labels are an important source of information for consumers to choose and decide whether to consume a product. In this case, the Appellee, based on the product label provided by the Appellants, believed that the Tieguanyin tea in question was produced by a specific manufacturer, Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd., using specific production processes, and formed a specific understanding of the quality and value of the tea. The Appellants' mislabeling misled the Appellee into purchasing the tea. The Appellants' argument that there was no need to counterfeit and that counterfeiting could not achieve any misleading effect contradicts the common knowledge that consumers rely on the contents of product labels for consumption. This argument does not stand. Pursuant to Articles 5, 37, and 38 of the Product Quality Law of the People's Republic of China, the Appellants, as sellers, have the obligation to ensure the truthfulness of the product labels they sell. Therefore, by selling tea that was not produced by Hangzhou Jujia Tea Co., Ltd. to the Appellee, and affixing a false hygiene license number that does not exist, the Appellants' conduct was fraudulent. Consequently, the Appellants' act of selling the tea in question to the Appellee constituted fraud.

2. Whether the statute of limitations had expired.
    The Appellee Su Xiangqian became aware of the infringement of his rights only on March 14, 2011, when the Xiaoshan Branch of the Hangzhou Municipal Bureau of Quality and Technical Supervision issued a reply to a third party, Zhang Jun, concerning the tea in question. The Appellee filed the lawsuit on March 10, 2012. Therefore, the Appellee's lawsuit did not exceed the two-year statute of limitations. Furthermore, regarding this dispute, the Appellee Su Xiangqian had repeatedly negotiated with the Appellants, Baihui Branch and Baixin Company. Therefore, the court does not support the Appellants' argument that the lawsuit exceeded the statute of limitations.

In conclusion, the first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly, and should be upheld. Accordingly, pursuant to Article 170, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Xuzhou Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on June 19, 2013:

The appeal is dismissed, and the original judgment is affirmed.

This judgment is final.
